items.title: Bill Easley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 1, 2021
items.q: lesson one is a lesson that I got from Joe Allard way back in 1964... Joe Allard who had you take your instrument... And he’d take you through a chromatic sequence of intervals.

ctx.x: Okay. You said — that’s a great story. You said something a couple of minutes ago that I want to follow up on. When he was asking you about the bridge to “I Got Rhythm” and you said basically that I know what to do but I don’t necessarily know what it is I’m doing. And in this day of intense jazz education where you can study for years and get a Ph.D., I’m wondering how that mindset jives with what we’re teaching now?

Well see I — at this late stage in my life I’d like to teach. But see like people in academia avoid me like the plague. You know? They have no interest in me, even though I’ve done this for sixty-some years. And I’ve pretty much accepted that by now. But I’ve had a couple of students near home, they come to my house, and I’m trying to teach as a language more so than a technical — even though see what Sonny Stitt told me about don’t worry about it, I didn’t — that does not mean that no, you shouldn’t learn. The…

always taught. I’m not saying I never taught because over the years somebody wanted to, “Man I’d like to study with you, I’d like to study.” So well the first problem I have, I don’t know what to charge you because I’ve never been a teacher so I don’t know what to charge. So lesson one is free. You come to my house and I’ll give you what I think is lesson one. I won’t charge. And lesson one is a lesson that I got from Joe Allard way back in 1964, you understand? items.title: Bill Easley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 1, 2021
items.q: I was just going part time, plus I was studying with Joseph Allard. I’m not sure if you know who Joseph Allard was, and that was a great, great, great person to run across at 18 years old you know.

ctx.x: So you learned to read and you became versatile, and when you got to New York you started hanging out, I mean did you — what was your first steady gig in music when you got to New York?

Okay, good question. In other words I worked and saved my money before I went to New York, you know, that summer. And even my sisters gave me a hundred dollars apiece. So I had it all figured — I knew how much money — and I went to Juilliard part time and I had my money set aside for how much my tuition was going to be. I was just going part time, plus I was studying with Joseph Allard. I’m not sure if you know who Joseph Allard was, and that was a great, great, great person to run across at 18 years old you…

but he called me. And he said, “Man you’ve got to — we’ll pick you up at your apartment house” and so on. So I had to go to my foreman and tell him, “Look man, I just got my big break in show business and I know I should give you two weeks notice.” But he said, “No I can’t start a prison.” So I quit my job and I go out and they are waiting for me uptown. And it was a four piece band and there were three girl dancer/singers. And so I hadn’t even met them before. And it’s like a station wagon with a trailer pulling…
